content: Services provided within certain models of care may result in interruptions to treatment due to the complexity of follow-up schedules. Effective data collection and reporting mechanisms for tuberculosis (TB) care processes and outcomes are particularly important in models not managed by healthcare workers or those not based in health facilities. A one-year-old child living with HIV, who is stable on antiretroviral therapy (ART), has clinic visits scheduled every two months for medication refills and check-ups. This child, being a household contact of a caregiver diagnosed with TB, is initiated on TB preventive therapy (TPT) consisting of six months of isoniazid during an ART clinic visit. At this visit, a TB diagnostic evaluation is conducted to rule out active TB disease, and standardized education is provided about TPT and its potential side effects. The caregiver is given a two-month supply of isoniazid, sufficient until the child’s next ART clinic visit. Another two-month supply of isoniazid is provided. This process is repeated at the four-month ART clinic visit, with an additional two-month supply of isoniazid dispensed. At the six-month ART clinic visit, the child is evaluated and documented as having completed TPT. For a stable 15-year-old adolescent living with HIV and on ART, clinic visits are scheduled every six months for medication refills and check-ups. TPT, consisting of six months of isoniazid, is initiated during an ART clinic visit, which also includes a TB diagnostic evaluation to rule out active TB disease and education about TPT and its potential side effects. The adolescent is provided with a six-month supply of isoniazid to last until the next ART clinic visit. At the six-month follow-up, the adolescent is evaluated and documented as having completed TPT. Programmatic support for TB care includes adherence support and screening for TB and adverse events, which should be provided at least monthly. This support can be delivered virtually, in the community, or through a combination of these methods to maintain differentiated service delivery (DSD) models and reduce contact with health facilities. Such support should complement clinical assessments conducted during in-person clinic visits. TPT assessments involve evaluating for breakthrough TB, monitoring weight, assessing for TPT-related adverse events, providing adherence counseling, and adjusting TPT dosages based on weight changes if necessary. The COVID-19 pandemic has significantly disrupted TB service delivery, reversing years of progress in reducing the TB disease burden. There has been a global decline in the number of people newly diagnosed with TB, with an associated increase in TB-related deaths. Children and adolescents have been disproportionately affected, with TB notifications in children under five years decreasing by 28% and in those aged 5–14 years by 21% between 2019 and 2020. Vulnerable groups, such as children and adolescents, are particularly impacted due to their dependence on adults for accessing healthcare. WHO has updated its guidance to help countries maintain continuity of TB services during health emergencies, emphasizing people-centered approaches and leveraging opportunities across diseases like TB and COVID-19. Less invasive sample collection methods should be prioritized to reduce transmission risks during procedures like sputum induction. Multimonth dispensing or community delivery of TB medicines can help achieve this. Routine HIV testing is recommended for all children and adolescents with presumed or diagnosed TB. All children living with HIV who are household contacts of individuals with infectious TB should be evaluated for TB disease and either treated for TB or provided with TPT if active TB is ruled out. Integrated and collaborative TB and HIV services are essential to identify and prevent disease in coinfected children. For children living with HIV, TB diagnosis can be more challenging due to overlapping clinical features with other diseases, reduced sensitivity of diagnostic tests like the tuberculin skin test (TST), and the high prevalence of other lung diseases. Diagnostic algorithms tailored for high-risk groups, including children living with HIV, should be used, and every effort should be made to confirm TB diagnosis through molecular tests on appropriate specimens. Urine-based lateral flow lipoarabinomannan (LF-LAM) testing can serve as a rapid diagnostic tool for children living with HIV with signs of TB, especially in urgent cases. Treatment of TB in children living with HIV involves a four-drug regimen (isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol) for two months, followed by a two-drug regimen (isoniazid and rifampicin) for four months. Treatment regimens may be adjusted based on disease severity. Dosages should be adjusted for weight gain during treatment. Most children living with HIV respond well to the six-month regimen if they adhere to treatment. Children living with HIV who successfully complete TB treatment may receive TPT to prevent future infections. However, treatment outcomes are generally poorer for children living with HIV compared to their HIV-negative counterparts, particularly in the absence of antiretroviral therapy (ART). Risk factors for poor outcomes include severe malnutrition, coinfections, severe immune suppression, and high viral load. Comprehensive care, including nutritional support and pyridoxine supplementation, is critical for improving outcomes in this population.
